::: {.pageinfo}
Needs: squares, square roots and one right triangle. The folded sections use calculus. Reading time: about 10 minutes, plus 10 for the folds.
:::

::: {.puzzle}
Espresso is brewed from grounds about a quarter of a millimetre across. French press uses grounds about a millimetre across. Same beans, four times the size.

Why does each brew method need its own size? And what does one click of the grinder's dial physically change?
:::

::: {.takeaways}
If you take away three things:

1. **A click slides the inner burr a fixed distance along the shaft.** The cutting surfaces are slanted, so the gap at the exit widens by a smaller, still fixed, amount per click. That gap caps the size of what comes out.
2. **A grind is a spread of sizes, not one size.** A main peak follows the gap. A second peak of *fines*, fragments of single cells about 25–50 µm across, stays where it is. Fines give up their flavor almost at once and slow the water down.
3. **Each brew method needs grounds whose diffusion time matches its contact time.** Diffusion time grows like the square of the particle size, so ten times the contact time calls for grounds about three times bigger.
:::

## The machine

A [burr grinder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burr_mill) crushes beans between two hardened cutters called *burrs*. In a *conical* burr grinder like the KINGrinder P0, the outer burr is a fixed ring and the inner burr is a cone that turns inside it when you crank the handle ([Counter Culture](https://counterculturecoffee.com/blogs/counter-culture-coffee/deep-dive-coffee-grinder-burrs)). Beans drop into the wide top of the space between them, where big blades crack them. The pieces are carried down a gap that narrows toward the bottom, and they leave through its narrowest part, the *exit gap*.

Set a number of clicks, then press **Grind**. Each piece that falls into the cup stands for the same volume of coffee, and the histogram on the right counts them. (1 µm, a *micrometre* or *micron*, is a thousandth of a millimetre.)

## What a click moves

The dial under the inner burr works like a nut on a screw. KINGrinder gives the P0 30 clicks per full turn of the dial and 0.0333 mm per click ([KINGrinder](https://www.kingrinder.com/store/products/p0)), so one full turn moves the burr 1 mm. Turning the dial toward zero raises the cone into the ring until the burrs touch. That touch point is *zero*, and the clicks count from it. Each click away from zero lowers the cone by

$$
s_1 = \frac{1\ \text{mm}}{30} \approx 33.3\ \mu\text{m}.
$$

The gap does not open by 33.3 µm per click, though. Look at the close-up: the inner surface slides *along the shaft* by $s = n\,s_1$ after $n$ clicks, but the gap is measured *straight across* the two surfaces, which lean at an angle $\theta$ to the shaft. In the right triangle formed by $s$, the gap $g$ and the surface, $g$ is the side opposite $\theta$:

$$
g = n\, s_1 \sin\theta .
$$

This relation is linear: every click adds the same amount of gap, and twice the clicks means twice the gap. Only the slope depends on the grinder.

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Proof</span> Why the gap grows by s·sin θ<span class="needs">uses: right-angle trigonometry</span></summary>

Model the two cutting surfaces near the exit as cones with the same half-angle $\theta$, which touch along the bottom zone at zero clicks. This is a modelling choice; real burrs differ in detail. Cut the grinder through its axis. Each surface becomes a straight line leaning at $\theta$ to the shaft, and at zero clicks the two lines coincide.

Lower the inner burr by $s$. Every point of its line moves straight down by $s$, so its new line is parallel to the old one. Pick a point $A$ on the outer line and let $A'$ be the point straight below it on the new inner line, so $|AA'| = s$. Drop a perpendicular from $A$ to the inner line, meeting it at $F$. The triangle $AFA'$ has a right angle at $F$. Its side $A'F$ lies along the inner line, so the angle at $A'$ is the angle between that line and the vertical, which is $\theta$. The side opposite $A'$ is $AF$, so by the definition of the sine, $|AF| = s\sin\theta$. Because the lines are parallel, $|AF|$ is the distance between them everywhere, which is the gap.

Two other lengths sometimes get called "the gap." The horizontal (radial) distance between the lines is $s\tan\theta$, which is slightly larger. A particle is stopped by the shortest distance between the surfaces, which is the perpendicular one, $s\sin\theta$. A flat-burr grinder has its two discs at right angles to the shaft, so $\theta = 90^\circ$ and there the gap equals the travel.
</details>
:::

KINGrinder does not publish $\theta$ for the P0. Honest Coffee Guide's chart for the P0 pairs clicks with microns at an almost constant 10.7 µm per click across all four brew methods ([Honest Coffee Guide, P0](https://honestcoffeeguide.com/kingrinder-p0-grind-settings/); computed in [numbers.py](numbers.py)). In our formula that slope means $\sin\theta = 10.7/33.3 \approx 0.32$, or $\theta \approx 19^\circ$, which is the default in the figure. A ratio that constant suggests the chart was made by a linear conversion rather than measured click by click, so treat 19° as a placeholder, not a measurement of the burr. With it, 60 clicks gives a gap of $60 \times 33.3 \times 0.326 \approx 650$ µm.

::: {.family}
Most conical grinders, hand or electric, use this same arrangement of a turning cone inside a fixed ring. Flat-burr grinders use two parallel discs instead. Their gap is set at right angles to the discs, so one unit of travel is one unit of gap, the case $\theta = 90^\circ$ of the formula.
:::

## What comes out is a spread

The histogram never shows a single bar. Two peaks appear.

- **The main peak** is the pieces that were broken down until they fit through the exit gap. Its position follows the gap. In the model it is centred on the gap, which is a modelling choice; real particles are not spheres, and a long piece can slip through endwise.
- **The fines peak** is made of particles under about 100 µm. It sits at 25–50 µm whatever the setting, because fines are fragments of single cells, and the cells of a roasted bean are 25–50 µm across ([Mo et al. 2023](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-42380-y)). When a particle shatters between the burrs, the cells along the break are torn open, and some come off as fragments.

In an espresso grind measured by Mo et al., about 29% of the coffee was fines. For coarser settings the model lowers that share in proportion to 1/gap. The reasoning is that smaller pieces mean more broken surface per gram, and so more fines. This is a plausible picture, not a measurement.

Fines matter far beyond their share, for two reasons.

- **They give up their flavor almost at once.** In a fragment smaller than a cell, every cell is broken open, and water simply washes the soluble material out. Bigger particles have to be extracted by *diffusion*, molecules spreading out through the particle by random motion, which is slow ([Gagné, *Dynamics of Coffee Extraction*](https://coffeeadastra.com/2019/01/29/the-dynamics-of-coffee-extraction/)).
- **They choke the flow.** How easily water passes through a bed of grounds is set mostly by the *smallest* particles. In the standard model of a packed bed, adding 20% fines at 40 µm to a bed of 300 µm grounds cuts the flow at a given pressure to about a fifth (fold below; [numbers.py](numbers.py)). This is why grinders that make more fines have to be set coarser for the same espresso flow ([Kaffeemacher](https://kaffeemacher.de/en/blogs/kaffeewissen/coffee-particle-distribution)).

At the coarse end sit the *boulders*. Their cores barely extract. In an experiment cited by Gagné, water reached only about 100 µm into a particle, about five layers of cells in his estimate ([Gagné, *Extracting Shells of Coffee*](https://coffeeadastra.com/2019/01/17/extracting-shells-of-coffee/)).

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Method</span> Why the smallest particles control the flow<span class="needs">uses: the Kozeny–Carman equation</span></summary>

Slow flow through a packed bed obeys [Darcy's law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darcy%27s_law): the flow per unit area is $q = k\,\Delta p/(\mu L)$. Here $\Delta p$ is the pressure across the bed, $L$ is its depth, $\mu$ is the viscosity of water, and $k$ is the bed's *permeability*. The [Kozeny–Carman equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kozeny%E2%80%93Carman_equation) (Kozeny 1927, Carman 1937) estimates $k$ from the grains. In Carman's form, which uses the grains' surface area per unit of grain volume $S_v$,

$$
k = \frac{\varepsilon^3}{5\,S_v^2\,(1-\varepsilon)^2},
$$

where $\varepsilon$ is the fraction of the bed that is open space. For spheres of diameter $d$, $S_v = 6/d$, which gives the familiar $k = d^2\varepsilon^3/\big(180(1-\varepsilon)^2\big)$. So at fixed packing, permeability grows like the square of the grain size.

For a mixture, add up surface and volume. If a volume fraction $f_i$ of the grains has diameter $d_i$, then
$$
S_v = \sum_i f_i \frac{6}{d_i} = \frac{6}{d_{32}}, \qquad d_{32} = \Big(\sum_i \frac{f_i}{d_i}\Big)^{-1},
$$
where $d_{32}$ is the [Sauter mean diameter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sauter_mean_diameter). Because each size enters as $f_i/d_i$, small grains carry heavy weight. With 20% of the volume at 40 µm and 80% at 300 µm, $d_{32} = 1/(0.2/40 + 0.8/300) \approx 130$ µm. Permeability then falls by $(130/300)^2 \approx 0.19$ compared with no fines. This assumes the packing $\varepsilon$ stays the same. In practice fines also fill the pores and migrate, which makes things worse.
</details>
:::

## Why each brew method needs its own size

Brewing is a race between two clocks. The first is the **contact time**, how long water and coffee are together, and the brew method sets it. An espresso shot runs about 25 s, by the Italian Espresso National Institute's standard ([Wikipedia, *Espresso*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Espresso)). A V60 pour-over takes 3 to 3½ minutes ([Coava](https://coavacoffee.com/brew-methods/v60)). A French press steeps for 4 minutes ([Seattle Coffee Gear](https://www.seattlecoffeegear.com/pages/product-resources/bodum-brazil-french-press-8-cup-product-guide)).

The second is the **diffusion time**, how long the flavor needs to get out of a particle. In a pure-diffusion model this time grows like the *square* of the particle's size: twice the size, four times the time (proof in the fold). Matching the two clocks gives a rule:

$$
d \propto \sqrt{T},
$$

where $d$ is the particle size and $T$ the contact time. Ten times the contact time calls for grounds $\sqrt{10} \approx 3.2$ times bigger.

The rule fixes ratios, so it needs one anchor. Anchor it at espresso: 25 s with about 250 µm grounds. Then it predicts the other three methods.

| Method | Contact time | Predicted size $250\ \mu\text{m}\sqrt{T/25\ \text{s}}$ | Usual range (Honest Coffee Guide) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Moka pot | ~1½ min (rough) | ≈ 470 µm | 360–660 µm |
| Pour-over | 3¼ min | ≈ 700 µm | 410–930 µm |
| French press | 4 min | ≈ 775 µm | 690–1300 µm |

All three predictions land inside the usual ranges ([Honest Coffee Guide](https://honestcoffeeguide.com/coffee-grind-size-chart/)). That is a rough check of one scaling law with one fitted number, not a proof. The ranges are guidance built from recipes, not lab measurements, and we found no standard figure for how long water flows through a moka pot's grounds, so its time is only an estimate.

Drag across the chart, or use the slider, to pick a particle size. The chart follows the grinder above until you touch it.

A green dashed cursor marks the chosen size."></canvas>

The last column is what you taste when you dial in. If the water leaves before the flavor is out, the cup is sour and thin. Grind finer and the diffusion clock speeds up. If the water stays long after the easy flavors are out, it pulls out bitter, harsh compounds. Grind coarser.

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Proof</span> Why diffusion time grows like size squared<span class="needs">uses: partial derivatives</span></summary>

Let $c(\mathbf{x}, t)$ be the concentration of a flavor compound inside a particle. Diffusion with a constant coefficient $D$ obeys
$$
\frac{\partial c}{\partial t} = D\,\nabla^2 c .
$$
Treat the particle as starting uniformly loaded and its surface as held at zero, meaning the outside water carries the compound away. Now compare a particle with its copy scaled up by a factor $\lambda$. Write $\tilde c(\mathbf{x}, t) = c(\mathbf{x}/\lambda,\ t/\lambda^2)$. By the chain rule, $\partial_t \tilde c = \lambda^{-2}\,\partial_t c$ and $\nabla^2 \tilde c = \lambda^{-2}\,\nabla^2 c$, so $\tilde c$ satisfies the same equation. It also has the same starting state and the same boundary condition on the scaled particle. By uniqueness of solutions to this problem, $\tilde c$ is *the* solution for the big particle. So the big particle at time $\lambda^2 t$ is in exactly the state of the small one at time $t$. In particular, the time to extract any fixed fraction scales like $\lambda^2$, that is, like $d^2$.

For a sphere of radius $R$ the solution is classical (Crank, *The Mathematics of Diffusion*, ch. 6). The fraction extracted after time $t$ is
$$
F(t) = 1 - \frac{6}{\pi^2}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^2}\, e^{-n^2\pi^2 D t / R^2}.
$$
Time enters only through $Dt/R^2$, which is the scaling again. For example, $F = 0.77$ at $Dt/R^2 = 0.1$, and $F = 0.92$ at $0.2$ ([numbers.py](numbers.py)).

Real coffee departs from this model in known ways. Broken cells at the surface wash out at once (the fines effect), so small particles get a head start that does not scale. Cells and pores are not uniform. In immersion the outside liquid fills up with coffee and stops being a perfect sink. Temperature and stirring differ between methods. Gagné's model of extraction, which includes several of these effects, is not a simple power law ([Gagné](https://coffeeadastra.com/2019/01/29/the-dynamics-of-coffee-extraction/)). So $d^2$ is the backbone of the story, not all of it.
</details>
:::

**Flow adds a second set of limits.** In *percolation* methods, water flows through a bed of grounds: espresso, moka and pour-over. There the grind also controls how fast water gets through. The bed's *permeability*, how easily water passes through it, grows like $d^2$ (see the fold in the previous section).

- **Espresso.** A bed fine enough to extract in 25 s resists flow strongly, so the machine pushes with a pump at 9 bar. One *bar* is about the pressure of the atmosphere. Nine bar is about 1800 times the push of the few centimetres of water standing in a pour-over cone: 5 cm of water presses at about 0.005 bar ([numbers.py](numbers.py)).
- **Moka pot.** Steam in the lower chamber pushes at about 1–2 bar ([Wikipedia, *Moka pot*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moka_pot), citing Navarini et al. 2009). That is a fifth to a ninth of espresso's push, one reason moka grinds sit coarser than espresso grinds.
- **Pour-over.** Gravity alone does the pushing. A finer grind both extracts faster *and* slows the drawdown, which lengthens the contact time. Both effects push in the same direction, which is why pour-over is so touchy about grind.
- **French press.** This is *immersion*: the coffee steeps in the water, and nothing has to flow through the bed. The limit comes at the end, when you press. Particles small enough to pass the metal mesh end up in the cup as grit ([Seattle Coffee Gear](https://www.seattlecoffeegear.com/pages/product-resources/bodum-brazil-french-press-8-cup-product-guide)). That is a reason to grind coarser than the diffusion clock alone asks for: its prediction of 775 µm sits near the bottom of the usual French press range.

## Back to the dial

To find your setting, start from a chart, then let taste steer. Honest Coffee Guide suggests 39–86 clicks for pour-over on the P0 ([Honest Coffee Guide, P0](https://honestcoffeeguide.com/kingrinder-p0-grind-settings/)). Brew, taste, and move a few clicks at a time: sour and thin means fewer clicks, bitter and harsh means more. Each click moves the main peak by about 11 µm (with θ = 19°), roughly 2% of a pour-over grind. That is why a few clicks is a gentle step.

## What we found

A click is a fixed slide of the inner burr along the shaft, and the slanted burr surfaces turn it into a smaller, fixed widening of the exit gap, $g = n\,s_1\sin\theta$. The gap moves the main peak of the grind; the fines, fragments of single cells, stay at 25–50 µm and dominate both fast extraction and flow resistance. Each brew method then picks the size whose diffusion time, growing like $d^2$, matches its contact time: anchored at espresso, $d \propto \sqrt{T}$ lands inside the usual ranges for moka, pour-over and French press, with pressure and filters setting the remaining limits.
